rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wārith is a Divine Name because everything belongs to God and ultimately returns to Him; the verse links divine inheritance with the passing away of creation.
rows.anchor: God is the Inheritor insofar as all things belong to Him and thus return unto Him in the end

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣiddīq means truthful, sincere, or loyal; the Quran applies it to Joseph, Idrīs, and Mary, and uses its plural for earnest believers.
rows.anchor: The Quran also uses this term to describe Joseph

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Ṣiddīq may describe people naturally and habitually honest, or those who constantly affirm the truth.
rows.anchor: the term refers to those who are honest by nature and habit

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Abraham was truthful in speech, promises, and deeds.
rows.anchor: Abraham is said to have been truthful in his speech, his promises, and his deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic tradition distinguishes a prophet, who receives a divine message, from a messenger, who brings new revelation or law; all messengers are prophets, though Quranic usage is less distinct.
rows.anchor: All messengers are prophets, but not all prophets are messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tradition regards Abraham as both messenger and prophet, while the Quran explicitly calls him a prophet; his messenger status is implicit in references to his scriptures.
rows.anchor: Abraham is considered both a messenger and a prophet in Islamic tradition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse opens Quranic accounts of Abraham confronting his father Azār and his people over idolatry.
rows.anchor: one of several Quranic accounts of Abraham’s confrontation with his father, Azār

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's argument is that worshipping an object unable to hear or see is irrational.
rows.anchor: an argument against idolatry that is repeated in various ways throughout the Quran

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Idols cannot distinguish worshippers from nonworshippers or hear their prayers, and worshipping something less capable than oneself is futile.
rows.anchor: they can neither distinguish those who worship them from those who do not nor hear the supplications of their devotees

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some identify the objects of worship as simple idols; al-Rāzī instead suggests they represented powerful stars or revered people thought able to intercede with God.
rows.anchor: they may have worshipped them as representatives of the stars

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī
rows.claim: To avail someone means to avert harm or bring benefit, neither of which idols can do.
rows.anchor: they cannot prevent or avert harm or bring benefit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's uniquely received knowledge is prophetic spiritual knowledge of God's Reality and the Hereafter, by which his father and people could be guided.
rows.anchor: The knowledge that Abraham claims to possess uniquely is the spiritual knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A son guiding his father overturns tribal expectations: spiritual authority depends neither on age nor lineage, answering appeals to ancestral custom.
rows.anchor: spiritual authority, unlike tribal authority, is not determined by age or lineage

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah repeatedly shows age irrelevant to God's will, through aged Zachariah and his barren wife conceiving and infant Jesus speaking.
rows.anchor: human age is shown to be irrelevant to the manifestation of God’s Will

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: The sound path means the correct religion by which salvation is attained.
rows.anchor: The sound path is understood to mean the path of correct religion

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: Worshipping Satan means obeying Satan's promptings toward sin and evil, since Abraham's people did not directly worship Satan.
rows.anchor: Worship not Satan is understood to mean that one should not obey Satan’s promptings toward sin and evil

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: Obeying another being by disobeying God is tantamount to worshipping that being.
rows.anchor: through an act of disobedience to God is tantamount to“worshipping” that being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Walī means friend or protector and denotes close allegiance, support, or love.
rows.anchor: Friend here translates walī, which can also mean “protector”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast with God's friends, especially in Sufi usage, frames saints as channels of divine grace and Satan's friends as channels of temptation.
rows.anchor: serve as channels of His Grace and Favor in this world

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī and Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Becoming Satan's associate entails separation from or repudiation by God; some commentators say Abraham fears this, while others say he knows it will happen.
rows.anchor: When one becomes a friend or associate of Satan, one is dissociated from or repudiated by God

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: The feared friendship may mean that Abraham's father will share Satan's company in Hell; it is not literal friendship, since Satan is humanity's enemy and abandons followers in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: his father will end up as a companion or cohabitant with Satan in Hellfire

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: The repeated address O my father signals love and earnest filial concern, rather than disrespect.
rows.anchor: the words he speaks are spoken out of love and earnest filial concern

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: The threat to stone Abraham generally means cursing or verbally attacking him; some commentators allow a literal threat of physical stoning.
rows.anchor: threatening to curse him or to “stone him with words”

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: The order to leave for a long while likely tells Abraham to go so he will be safe from his father's punishment.
rows.anchor: Take leave of me so that you will be safe from my punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Peace is a greeting of believers in this world and Paradise and a prescribed response to ignorant or idle speech.
rows.anchor: the greeting of the believers, both in this world and in Paradise

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: Here Abraham's peace is not a greeting but a promise to end the confrontation without fighting and to reassure his father.
rows.anchor: an indication that he will discontinue his confrontation with his father

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham asks forgiveness for his father, but later disavows him once his enmity toward God becomes clear.
rows.anchor: when it became clear to him that his father was an enemy of God, he repudiated him

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Abraham promises to leave his family and their idols, understood by some as departing for the Holy Land.
rows.anchor: This is understood as his taking leave of his family to migrate to the Holy Land

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Although shaqiyyan can mean one who suffers perdition in the Hereafter, here it more likely means that God will answer Abraham's supplications, as in Zachariah's similar statement.
rows.anchor: more likely means that God will answer his prayers and supplications

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: Abraham's prayer likely asks for family and children to strengthen him after separation; Isaac and Jacob are the answer, fitting the sūrah's theme of blessed children as divine compassion.
rows.anchor: Abraham is said to have called upon his Lord to grant him family and children

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: An alternative says Abraham prayed for his father's guidance, but the author finds this less likely because the Quran says that guidance did not occur.
rows.anchor: this seems less likely, since according to the Quran this guidance does not come to pass

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isaac and Jacob are elsewhere described as God's gifts to Abraham; other passages give variant glad tidings of descendants.
rows.anchor: Isaac and Jacob are also described as gifts bestowed upon Abraham by God

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Each made a prophet includes Abraham as well as Isaac and Jacob; the two sons compensate him for losing his father and people, and are a better gift.
rows.anchor: the gift of these two prophets was far better than what he had lost

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: God's mercy bestowed on Abraham and his family may mean worldly bounty and provision, while others include prophethood and revelation.
rows.anchor: others say that it also refers to the gifts of prophethood and revelation

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: Lisāna ṣidqin ʿaliyyan idiomatically means the family's high reputation and sincere praise among many faiths, fulfilling Abraham's prayer for renown among later generations.
rows.anchor: the phrase refers to the high reputation and sincere praise that Abraham and his family enjoyed

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: He reads withdrawal from worldly creatures as a Sufi path to spiritual knowledge and holy gifts; solitude is needed at first, but later disciples should mix with people to deepen understanding.
rows.anchor: withdrawing from creatures is a necessary condition at the beginning of the path for Sufi disciples

rows.speaker: Abu’l-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī
rows.claim: He cites the verse to describe solitude's spiritual fruits; the quoted truthful tongue suggests honesty, while the verse's phrase idiomatically denotes renown.
rows.anchor: Shaykh Abu’l-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī (d. 656/1258) cited this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses is devoted to worshipping God alone without hypocrisy; Sufi sincerity means worship solely for God rather than worldly or afterlife rewards.
rows.anchor: to the One God, worshipping Him alone

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Mukhliṣ, devoted, and mukhlaṣ, specially chosen, are both valid readings.
rows.anchor: both can be considered correct according to al-Ṭabarī

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses is a messenger because he brought the Torah and a new divine law, and a prophet to Israelites and Pharaoh's people because he warned both.
rows.anchor: he brings his people a new scripture (the Torah) and through it a new Divine Law

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran recounts Moses in many other major passages.
rows.anchor: For other major accounts of Moses

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: The Mount is Sinai, and its right side is the side Moses saw as he approached from Midian and saw the burning bush.
rows.anchor: the side of the mountain that was on the right as Moses approached it from Midian

rows.speaker: Sufi commentators
rows.claim: The mountain's right side can symbolize the heart's innermost dimension, the locus of divine self-revelation and intimate discourse.
rows.anchor: a symbol for the innermost dimension of the heart

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Moses being drawn near is variously explained as hearing the pen write the Torah tablets, hearing God's speech directly, or being raised to a noble station; some prefer speaking of a station outside revelation to avoid implying spatial distance from God.
rows.anchor: For some, the latter interpretation is preferable, since it avoids the theological impossibility of discussing physical distance

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī and others
rows.claim: A mystical account says seventy thousand veils of light and darkness separated the Throne and earth, with only one veil between Moses and God.
rows.anchor: there are seventy thousand veils of light and darkness between the Throne and the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Intimate discourse likely means God spoke directly to Moses, the basis for his title Kalīm Allāh.
rows.anchor: a reference to God speaking to Moses directly

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Aaron was reportedly older than Moses, so the gift of Aaron means the gift of his prophethood; Aaron supported Moses' revelation rather than bringing a separate one, and was not a messenger.
rows.anchor: God’s giving Aaron to Moses is understood, therefore, to mean that He gave him the gift of Aaron’s prophethood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses say Moses and Aaron jointly received the Criterion, signs, authority, and the clarifying Book.
rows.anchor: Aaron along with Moses is said to have been given the Criterion

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: Aaron's appointment answers Moses' prayer for a family helper and brother who could speak more eloquently.
rows.anchor: God’s sending Aaron as a helper for Moses is said to come in response to Moses’ supplication

rows.speaker: Sufi commentators
rows.claim: Aaron represents revelation's esoteric dimension and is compared with ʿAlī's relation to the Prophet in the hadith that excludes any prophet after Muhammad.
rows.anchor: Aaron is said to represent the esoteric dimension of the revelation given to Moses

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Ishmael is considered both messenger and prophet, presumably for bringing Abrahamic monotheism to Arabia, especially the Jurhum tribe.
rows.anchor: he was responsible for bringing Abrahamic monotheism to the people of Arabia

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī and others
rows.claim: Being true to the promise refers to keeping his word; a report says he waited days or a full year for someone who forgot their meeting, and a similar story is told of Muhammad before prophethood.
rows.anchor: someone had asked Ishmael to wait for him in a specified location, and then forgot about him

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Those who identify Ishmael as the son nearly sacrificed in the Quran also understand his promise-keeping as steadfastness during that ordeal.
rows.anchor: may also allude to his remaining steadfast during this ordeal

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī and others
rows.claim: Ishmael pleased God through obedience, righteousness, purity, and avoiding ugly conduct; this recalls Zachariah's desired son and John's description.
rows.anchor: as a result of his obedience, righteousness, purity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer and almsgiving are duties for Muslims and are also commanded to the People of the Book; some say Ishmael prescribed night prayer and daytime charity.
rows.anchor: Some say Ishmael used to command his people to perform prayer at night and give charity during the day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idrīs is truthful and a prophet like Abraham, and is included among the patient elsewhere.
rows.anchor: Idrīs is also mentioned along with Ishmael and Dhu’l-Kifl in

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some derive Idrīs's name from studying because of his love of study; al-Zamakhsharī questions that etymology.
rows.anchor: Some say that his name is derived from the root d-r-s

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Idrīs is usually identified as Enoch, Noah's great-grandfather, but sometimes identified with the Quranic Elias.
rows.anchor: Idrīs is most commonly considered the great-grandfather of Noah

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: Traditions credit antediluvian Idrīs with first writing by pen, astronomy, mathematics, sewn clothing, and the epithet father of sages; some call him Adam's first prophet and say he received thirty scrolls.
rows.anchor: Idrīs is said to have been the first to have written with a pen

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: His raised station is variously said to mean bodily or spiritual ascent to the fourth or sixth heaven; a hadith reports the Prophet met him in the fourth on the Ascension.
rows.anchor: raised him either bodily or in spirit to the fourth or sixth heaven

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some say Idrīs remains alive, taken up by God like Jesus; another explanation is simply that his station was prophethood.
rows.anchor: Idrīs has not yet died, having been raised alive

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī and others
rows.claim: They refers to all prophets and sacred figures previously named in the sūrah.
rows.anchor: They refers to all of the prophets and sacred figures mentioned to this point in the sūrah

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Progeny of Adam may include all the figures or specifically Idrīs, who predates Noah and Abraham and fits none of the other groups.
rows.anchor: Progeny of Adam may refer to all of these figures or specifically to Idrīs

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī and others
rows.claim: Those carried with Noah means Abraham and descendants Isaac, Ishmael, and Jacob; Israel's progeny means Moses, Aaron, Zachariah, John, Mary, and Jesus.
rows.anchor: Those whom We carried with Noah refers to Abraham and his progeny, Isaac, Ishmael, and Jacob

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs are proofs from revealed books, and the prophets prostrated and wept in humility; a hadith has the Prophet command Quran recitation with weeping, even self-induced.
rows.anchor: Weeping is indicated in several aḥādīth as the appropriate response to hearing the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is one of fifteen sajdah verses, upon whose recitation Muslims are enjoined to prostrate; scholars disagree whether prostration after 41:37–38 and 53:62 is obligatory, and commonly regard 38:24 as thanksgiving rather than obligation.
rows.anchor: this verse is one of fifteen verses known as sajdah (prostration) verses

rows.speaker: al-Qushayrī
rows.claim: Prostration and weeping express tender-heartedness shared by prophets, while bodily prostration reflects inner submission to realized spiritual truths.
rows.anchor: Qushayrī, was shared by all the prophets

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Responding this way is the first stage of divine love, later replaced by joy in hearing the Beloved's words as spiritual nearness grows.
rows.anchor: characteristic of the first stage of the love of God

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: He identifies the generation succeeding the prophets as the Jews.
rows.anchor: the generation who succeeded the prophets mentioned in v. 58 refers to the Jews

rows.speaker: Mujāhid and Qatādah
rows.claim: They identify that generation as the Muslim community at the end of time.
rows.anchor: it refers to the Muslim community at the end of time

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Neglecting prayer may mean abandoning prayer altogether, or delaying it beyond its appointed time.
rows.anchor: others suggest that it means that they failed to say the prayers at their appointed time

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Ghayy may mean requital or punishment, be glossed as evil, or name a valley, well, or river in Hell.
rows.anchor: will meet the requital or punishment for their error

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The door of repentance remains open to those people until death.
rows.anchor: the door of repentance remains open until death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly pairs belief and righteous action as indispensable, interconnected bases for the Garden, for Muslims and followers of other faiths.
rows.anchor: the twin bases for attaining to the Garden in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly affirms that God does not wrong people.
rows.anchor: other verses asserting that God does not wrong people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gardens of Eden are the gardens of the Hereafter, concealed from humans in worldly life; God's promise is entry into the Garden for His servants and friends and is certain to come true.
rows.anchor: They are in the Unseen because they remain hidden to human beings while they are in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise has no idle talk, and its greeting is Peace; the Quran describes both features in other passages.
rows.anchor: The notion of the paradisal Garden as a place in which there is no idle talk

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Paradise's provision includes food, drink, and everything desired; some say there is no night or midday, with time marked by the veils and gates opening and closing.
rows.anchor: There they shall have their provision of food and drink and all that they desire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse reportedly followed a revelation hiatus of twelve, fifteen, or forty nights, when the Prophet was asked about the Cave's people, Dhu’l-Qarnayn, and the Spirit; the delay troubled him and idolaters said God had abandoned him.
rows.anchor: there had been an unusually long period—reportedly twelve, fifteen, or forty nights

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Gabriel returned, the Prophet reportedly asked why he did not visit more often; the verse gives Gabriel's response, and its opening We refers to the archangel.
rows.anchor: The present verse is understood to represent Gabriel’s direct response to the Prophet’s question

rows.speaker: minority interpretation
rows.claim: A minority reads the speaker as the people of Paradise, who settle there only by God's command.
rows.anchor: A minority interpretation understands this verse to convey the words of the people of the Garden

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Before and behind may refer to temporal periods—world and Hereafter, before creation and after annihilation, or past and future—or spatially to earth and Heaven; what lies between may be the two trumpet blasts or earthly life, showing God's command of all time and space.
rows.anchor: God’s possession of these three temporal or spatial dimensions indicates His encompassing all time and space

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not forgetful reassures the Prophet that God has not forgotten him; revelation's intervals are providential and ultimately beneficial.
rows.anchor: any interval between the revelations is providential and for his ultimate benefit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lord of the heavens and the earth is a Quranic title for God.
rows.anchor: Lord of the heavens and the earth is a title for God found also

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī
rows.claim: The closing question may ask whether anyone equals God in generosity and bounty, or whether any partner can be named beside Him.
rows.anchor: Is there any who is His equal or His like in generosity and bounty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question is rhetorical: no one besides God should be called God and idols are not gods; some commentators say none besides Him should be called al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: indicating that no one should be called

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers' rhetorical question dismisses resurrection, and the response is that God's ability to create people initially proves He can recreate them.
rows.anchor: God’s ability to create human beings the first time should be sufficient proof that He can do it again

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers are allies of human or jinn satans who inspire them, and will be brought with them to Hell, as other verses say Hell will be filled with Satan's followers.
rows.anchor: These satans can also be either human beings or jinn

rows.speaker: Quran commentators
rows.claim: Being brought to Hell on one's knees expresses fear, humiliation, and helplessness before judgment; compare wrongdoers left kneeling and communities kneeling on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: a posture reflecting their state of fear, lowliness, and powerlessness

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Every group means each religious community or nation; the phrase also refers to communities that fell into error or schism.
rows.anchor: From every group means from every religious community or nation

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: The most insolent, most deserving to burn are often identified as misguided leaders who lead their communities astray and merit greater punishment.
rows.anchor: the leaders of those communities in error, who are not only astray themselves, but who lead their communities astray as well

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Alternatives identify them as the most stubborn in disbelief and disobedience, or the worst offenders such as idolaters and disbelievers, who enter the Fire first.
rows.anchor: those who are most stubborn in their rejection of God and in disobedience to Him

rows.speaker: Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Although verses 69–70 describe disbelievers in the Fire, these verses indicate that both pious and wicked people approach Hell.
rows.anchor: all people, both the pious and the iniquitous, will approach it

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some say Hell's flames subside or cool for the righteous so they pass unaware; others say they enter and later emerge because of good deeds.
rows.anchor: its flames will subside or become cool for them

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Other views say the Fire never touches the righteous, only disbelievers are addressed, or approaching Hell means experiencing fever and illness in this world.
rows.anchor: Others assert that the Fire will not touch the righteous at all as they pass through Hell

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Another view has believers pass through the Fire to appreciate God's bounty more fully and enjoy greater happiness in the Garden.
rows.anchor: so that they may know the extent of God’s Bounty and Favor toward them

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet says those present at Badr and Ḥudaybiyah will not enter the Fire; when Ḥafṣah asks about this verse, he answers by reciting the next verse about saving the reverent.
rows.anchor: In aḥadīth, the Prophet declares that none of those present

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Makkan setting, disbelievers are Quraysh idolaters and believers are the Prophet's Companions; Quraysh boast of better homes and more prominent associates, assuming earthly advantages will persist in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The Makkan idolaters boast of their being better in station

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recurring destruction of earlier generations warns Quraysh that material wealth and status cannot protect wrongdoers from punishment; those earlier peoples had more than the Makkans yet were destroyed.
rows.anchor: were destroyed for their wrongdoing, despite having a better earthly provision and material situation than the Makkans

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This answers the disbelievers' claim in the previous verse that they surpassed believers in station and company.
rows.anchor: a response to the implicit claim of the disbelievers in v. 73

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Longevity, like wealth and status, cannot protect people from punishment; it may give a chance to repent, but can instead extend misguidance and sin, ending in a sudden seizure.
rows.anchor: God’s prolonging the lives or delaying the destruction of some disbelievers and wrongdoers may not necessarily be a blessing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised punishment or Hour means either destruction of a particular community in this life or the universal Last Day and Judgment.
rows.anchor: their sudden end may come through either the earthly destruction of their particular community or the universal onset of the events of the Last Day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God further guides the already guided and increases the faith of believers, while increasing disease in diseased hearts; the verses point to the interaction of divine and human will, and God may leave those choosing evil to their own misguidance.
rows.anchor: Such verses point to a certain nexus between the role of Divine and human will

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Increase in guidance may mean help in obedience, spiritual or material favors, stronger certainty and resolve, or new revealed signs; historically it may refer to successive guidance and abrogation of earlier rulings for the changing Muslim community.
rows.anchor: God may increase people in guidance by helping them in acts of obedience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Righteous deeds endure and surpass worldly goods in reward and benefit; here they may mean obligatory or extra prayers and praise, whose rewards in both worlds exceed the idolaters' status and company.
rows.anchor: Regarding the enduring reward and benefit of righteous deeds in comparison to the material goods of this world
